from.place: Proof, second paragraph: “localization and strict henselization preserve excellence”; through Greco Theorem 5.3(iii)-(iv) and Lemma 5.5, the universally catenary normalization dimension input is the finite-birational specialization of Stacks Tag 02IJ. This node states the general dimension formula used in that specialization.

title: Dimension formula for finite type extensions of universally catenary domains
statement: Let $R\subset S$ be an inclusion of commutative domains, with $R$ Noetherian [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring] and universally catenary [def-exc-excellent-ring], and with $S$ a finite type $R$-algebra [def-weil-pbc-finite-type-algebra]. A domain is a nonzero ring without zero divisors. Let $\mathfrak p\subset R$ and $\mathfrak q\subset S$ be prime ideals with $\mathfrak q\cap R=\mathfrak p$. For a prime $\mathfrak r$ of a ring $A$, put $\kappa(\mathfrak r)=\operatorname{Frac}(A/\mathfrak r)$ and write $\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak r)$ for the supremum of lengths of strict chains of prime ideals ending at $\mathfrak r$. Write $\operatorname{trdeg}_A B$ for transcendence degree [def-kun-transcendence-degree]. Then $$\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak q)+\operatorname{trdeg}_{\kappa(\mathfrak p)}\kappa(\mathfrak q)=\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak p)+\operatorname{trdeg}_R S.$$

source.place: Tag 02IJ (lemma-dimension-formula), equality clause for a universally catenary base; lines 27520–27607.

proof.text:
Fix a field $F$ and a prime $Q$ of $F[T]$. The cited PID statement shows that if $Q
e0$, then $Q=(f)$ for a nonzero nonunit $f$. Primality makes $f$ irreducible: in $f=ab$, one factor belongs to $(f)$ and cancellation shows that the other is a unit. Every ideal containing $(f)$ is $(g)$ with $g\mid f$, hence is $(f)$ or the whole ring. Thus every nonzero prime is maximal; since $F[T]$ is a domain, $\operatorname{ht}(0)=0$ and $\operatorname{ht}(Q)=1$ for $Q
e0$. If $Q=0$, its residue field is $F(T)$ and $\{T\}$ is a transcendence basis: polynomial evaluation is injective and this element generates the rational function field. Hence its transcendence degree over $F$ is one. If $Q
e0$, writing $	heta$ for the image of $T$, the residue field is $F(	heta)$ with $f(	heta)=0$. The cited power-basis theorem makes it finite-dimensional; for each element, its first $d+1$ powers in dimension $d$ are dependent, so the extension is algebraic, and the cited zero-degree criterion gives degree zero. Consequently in both cases $\operatorname{ht}(Q)+\operatorname{trdeg}_F\kappa(Q)=1$.

source.place: Tag 02IJ, Case I, the two possibilities for a prime in the polynomial fibre; PID and power-basis inputs expanded.

proof.text: For a domain $R$, put $P=R[T]$, $F=\operatorname{Frac}(R)$ and $G=\operatorname{Frac}(P)$. The polynomial-domain node makes these fraction fields legitimate. Clearing a common denominator in the finitely many coefficients identifies $G$ with $F(T)$. Every fraction $a/b$ in $F$ is algebraic over $R$, by the nonzero polynomial $bY-a$, and similarly every element of $G$ is algebraic over $P$. Thus no nonempty family in either extension is algebraically independent, and their algebra transcendence degrees are zero by definition. Apply the domain tower identity to $R\subseteq P\subseteq G$ and $R\subseteq F\subseteq G$. The first gives $\operatorname{trdeg}_R G=\operatorname{trdeg}_R P+0$ and the second gives $\operatorname{trdeg}_R G=0+\operatorname{trdeg}_F G=1$, the last value being Step 1 at the zero prime. Hence $\operatorname{trdeg}_R P=1$.

source.place: Tag 02IJ, Case I, initial assertion trdeg_R R[x]=1; domain tower identity expands the fraction-field convention.

proof.text: Assume now that $R$ is a Noetherian universally catenary commutative domain and consider $R\subseteq P=R[T]$. The coefficient description of polynomials exhibits $P$ as the free $R$-module on $1,T,T^2,\ldots$, so it is flat by the free-module clause of the cited flatness theorem. It is a finite type algebra (generated by $T$), hence Noetherian by the cited finite-type theorem. For a prime $\mathfrak q$ above $\mathfrak p$, apply the flat height formula, with both rings Noetherian, to obtain $\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak q)=\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak p)+\operatorname{ht}(\bar{\mathfrak q})$, where $\bar{\mathfrak q}=\mathfrak q/\mathfrak pP$ is a prime of $(R/\mathfrak p)[T]$. The displayed identification sends each polynomial to its coefficient classes: its kernel is exactly the polynomials with all coefficients in $\mathfrak p$, namely $\mathfrak pP$.

source.place: Tag 02IJ, Case I, flat base-fibre dimension formula.

proof.text: Put $D=R/\mathfrak p$, $W=D\setminus\{0\}$ and $F=\operatorname{Frac}(D)=\kappa(\mathfrak p)$. The coefficient map $D[T]\to F[T]$ is localization at $W$: it is injective, elements of $W$ become units, and a common denominator for the finitely many coefficients writes each polynomial as $g/w$. Since $\bar{\mathfrak q}\cap D=0$, the localization-prime theorem gives a prime $Q=\bar{\mathfrak q}F[T]$ and identifies the entire prime interval below $\bar{\mathfrak q}$ with the interval below $Q$. Indeed every prime contained in $\bar{\mathfrak q}$ avoids $W$, and extension and contraction preserve inclusion, so chains in the two intervals have the same lengths. Hence $\operatorname{ht}(\bar{\mathfrak q})=\operatorname{ht}(Q)$. Its residue-field clause identifies $\kappa(\mathfrak q)=\operatorname{Frac}(P/\mathfrak q)=\operatorname{Frac}(D[T]/\bar{\mathfrak q})$ with $\kappa(Q)$ over $F$; the equality with the local-quotient definition is the fraction map $(a\bmod\bar{\mathfrak q})/(s\bmod\bar{\mathfrak q})\mapsto a/s\bmod\bar{\mathfrak q}D[T]_{\bar{\mathfrak q}}$, whose denominator is nonzero precisely when $s\notin\bar{\mathfrak q}$. Now Steps 1 and 3 give $\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak q)+\operatorname{trdeg}_{\kappa(\mathfrak p)}\kappa(\mathfrak q)=\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak p)+1$, which is the item for $P$ by Step 2.

source.place: Tag 02IJ, Case I, passage to the polynomial fibre over kappa(p); localization prime correspondence (Tag 00E3).

proof.text: Next let $R\subseteq S=R[\theta]$ with a nonzero kernel $\mathfrak n$ for $P=R[T]\twoheadrightarrow S$, $T\mapsto\theta$. The kernel is prime since $S$ is a domain, and $\mathfrak n\cap R=0$ since $R\subseteq S$. Choose a nonzero polynomial in $\mathfrak n$; it stays nonzero over $F=\operatorname{Frac}(R)$ and annihilates $\theta$ in $\operatorname{Frac}(S)=F(\theta)$, the equality following by taking fractions of polynomials in $\theta$. The power-basis theorem makes this a finite field extension of $F$. Every element of $S$ is therefore algebraic over $F$ (linear dependence of its powers); clearing the finitely many coefficient denominators gives a nonzero annihilating polynomial over $R$. Thus no nonempty family in $S$ is algebraically independent over $R$, and $\operatorname{trdeg}_R S=0$. For $\mathfrak q\subset S$ let $\mathfrak q'$ be its inverse image in $P$. The quotient map identifies $P/\mathfrak q'$ with $S/\mathfrak q$, so their fraction fields, and hence residue fields, agree over $\kappa(\mathfrak p)$, where $\mathfrak p=\mathfrak q\cap R$.

source.place: Tag 02IJ, Case II, generic transcendence degree zero and the prime q above the quotient kernel.

proof.text: The map $P\to F[T]$ is localization at $R\setminus\{0\}$ by the same common-denominator verification as Step 4, and is injective by the polynomial-domain statement. The prime $\mathfrak n$ avoids these denominators and has nonzero extension $N$ in $F[T]$ (a nonzero element of $\mathfrak n$ remains nonzero). Every prime below $\mathfrak n$ also avoids the denominators. Extension and contraction therefore identify all chains below $\mathfrak n$ with all chains below $N$, using the prime-bijection clause. By Step 1, $\operatorname{ht}(N)=1$, so $\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak n)=1$.

source.place: Tag 02IJ, Case II, height-one kernel via localization to F[x].

proof.text: The polynomial algebra $P$ is finite type over $R$, hence catenary by the universal-catenarity clause of the cited definition. In the interval $[0,\mathfrak q']$ chain lengths have a finite upper bound and all saturated chains have equal length. A finite chain in any subinterval can be refined to a saturated one by choosing an extension of maximal length among the bounded integer lengths. Choose a saturated chain from $\mathfrak n$ to $\mathfrak q'$ of length $l$. By Step 6, $0\subsetneq\mathfrak n$ is saturated. Prefixing it gives a saturated chain from $0$ to $\mathfrak q'$ of length $1+l$. Every chain ending at $\mathfrak q'$ can first be prefixed by $0$ (if necessary) and then refined; catenarity says its resulting saturated length is $1+l$. Thus $\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak q')=1+l$. Primes of $S=P/\mathfrak n$ correspond to primes of $P$ containing $\mathfrak n$: inverse image under the quotient and $J\mapsto J/\mathfrak n$ are inverse inclusion-preserving maps, since primality on both sides is the assertion that the same quotient ring $P/J$ is a domain. This identifies the interval $[0,\mathfrak q]$ with $[\mathfrak n,\mathfrak q']$. Refinement and the same catenarity condition show that every maximal chain there has length $l$, so $\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak q)=l$. Consequently $\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak q')=\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak q)+1$.

source.place: Tag 02IJ, last paragraph of Case II; Tag 00NI/00NL catenary and universally catenary definitions, saturated-chain argument expanded.

proof.text: Apply the polynomial formula of Step 4 to $\mathfrak q'$. With $t=\operatorname{trdeg}_{\kappa(\mathfrak p)}\kappa(\mathfrak q)$, Steps 5 and 7 give $(\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak q)+1)+t=\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak p)+1$ and $\operatorname{trdeg}_R S=0$. All the heights here are finite integers: universal catenarity bounds chains from the zero prime in $R$, in $P$, and in $S$ (each a finite type $R$-algebra). The number $t$ is either zero or one by Step 1. Cancelling one gives $\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak q)+t=\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak p)$, the required formula in the quotient case. Together with the zero-kernel case of Step 4 this proves the formula for every one-generator domain extension over any Noetherian universally catenary domain.

source.place: Tag 02IJ, conclusion of Case II equality.

proof.text: Induct strongly on a finite list of algebra generators for $S$ over $R$, supplied by the finite-type definition. For zero generators $S=R$, the two primes and residue fields agree, and both relevant transcendence degrees are zero because every element is annihilated by a polynomial $Y-a$ over its base. For $n>0$, set $A=R[x_1,\ldots,x_{n-1}]\subseteq S=A[x_n]$ and $\mathfrak r=\mathfrak q\cap A$. Then $A$ is a domain and is Noetherian by the finite-type Noetherian theorem. It is universally catenary: every finite type $A$-algebra is finite type over $R$, by adjoining its generators to the displayed generators of $A$, so is catenary by the definition for $R$. Apply the induction hypothesis to $R\subseteq A$ and the one-generator result of Step 8 to $A\subseteq S$. Write $a=\operatorname{trdeg}_{\kappa(\mathfrak p)}\kappa(\mathfrak r)$, $b=\operatorname{trdeg}_{\kappa(\mathfrak r)}\kappa(\mathfrak q)$, $d=\operatorname{trdeg}_R A$ and $e=\operatorname{trdeg}_A S$. The two formulas read $\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak r)+a=\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak p)+d$ and $\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak q)+b=\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak r)+e$. All numbers are finite: $d$ is finite inductively, $e\in\{0,1\}$ by the one-generator proof, heights are finite by catenarity, and each residue degree is finite by the corresponding equality. Adding and cancelling $\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak r)$ yields $\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak q)+(a+b)=\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak p)+(d+e)$. The field tower identity identifies $a+b$ with the residue-field degree of the item; the domain tower identity identifies $d+e$ with $\operatorname{trdeg}_R S$. This is the asserted formula.
